units.t: Spotting Manipulation. Episode one.
In this episode: How manipulators work, Gaslighting, The dark triad and How cults recruit.
Part one. How manipulators work.
Manipulation works because it's hard to see from the inside.
Learn the common tactics and they lose much of their power.
Influence versus manipulation.
We all try to influence each other.
Manipulation is different: it exploits emotions, hides intentions or distorts information so you act against your own interests.
A useful test is whether the tactic would still work if you fully understood it.
Honest persuasion would; manipulation usually wouldn't.
Most people use a little pressure now and then, but a manipulator shows a repeated pattern.
Therapist Susan Forward, in her 1997 book Emotional Blackmail, described the tactic as FOG: fear, obligation and guilt.
'After everything I've done for you…' creates obligation, and 'If you leave, I don't know what I'll do' uses fear and guilt.
The warning sign is when threats of sulking, anger or withdrawal regularly steer your choices.
Love bombing and urgency.
Love bombing means intense flattery, gifts, constant contact and talk of destiny, very early in a relationship.
The term was first used in the 1970s for how some cults welcomed recruits.
It creates a strong bond before you know the person well enough to judge them, and affection may later be withdrawn as leverage.
Genuine affection grows at a reasonable pace and respects your friendships.
Pressure tactics work similarly: 'This offer ends tonight.'
Under time pressure, people lean on quick emotional reactions rather than weighing evidence.
Scammers, pushy salespeople and controlling partners use urgency, and many Australian phone and text scams claim a bank account, parcel or tax debt needs action within hours.
Make a personal rule to sleep on significant decisions.
Legitimate offers will survive a day's wait.
Blame and isolation.
Psychologist Jennifer Freyd described DARVO: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.
You raise a genuine concern, and within minutes you're the one apologising.
Related moves include changing the subject, bringing up your past mistakes or calling you 'too sensitive'.
If raising any problem reliably turns into a discussion of your faults, take that pattern seriously.
One of the most serious warning signs is gradual isolation: criticising your friends, making family visits awkward, sulking when you go out, or monitoring your phone.
It removes outside perspectives and increases dependence, and it creeps in as small complaints.
Manipulators may also tell different stories to different people, called triangulation.
Staying connected to trusted people is one of your best protections.
When it becomes abuse.
Manipulation can shade into abuse.

Coercive control is an ongoing pattern of behaviour that takes away a person's freedom: tracking their movements, controlling money, restricting who they see, making threats and wearing down their confidence.
It often involves no physical violence, which is why it can go unrecognised for years.
Research on domestic homicides has found that coercive control frequently precedes physical violence.
New South Wales made coercive control in current and former intimate relationships a criminal offence from July 2024, and Queensland's similar offence took effect in 2025.
Other jurisdictions are developing their own approaches.
Protecting yourself.
Recognising a tactic is powerful: once you think 'this is false urgency', the pressure fades.
Slow decisions down.
Talk things over with someone outside the situation.
Notice patterns rather than single incidents, and consider keeping a private note of what happens.
You can say no without a long justification.
If someone's behaviour includes threats, control or fear, it may be abuse.
In Australia you can contact 1800RESPECT, 1800 737 732, a free, confidential service available 24 hours a day, for advice about your situation or someone else's.
In an emergency, or if you're in immediate danger, call 000.
The key idea: Manipulation relies on you not noticing what's happening, and emotional blackmail works through fear, obligation and guilt.
Part two. Gaslighting.
Making someone doubt their own memory and sanity.
Where the word comes from, how it works, and how to keep your footing.
Where the word comes from.
In Patrick Hamilton's 1938 play Gas Light, and the 1944 film Gaslight starring Ingrid Bergman, a husband secretly dims the gas lights and hides objects, then insists his wife is imagining things.
He wants to hide his crimes and keep control.
Slowly she starts to believe she's losing her mind.
Gaslighting now describes a pattern that makes someone doubt their own perceptions, memory or judgement, and Merriam-Webster named it word of the year in 2022.
Common tactics include flatly denying things, 'I never said that', trivialising feelings, 'You're too sensitive', countering memories and shifting blame.
Some gaslighters tell others the target is 'confused', weakening outside support.
The pattern, repeated over months, does the damage.
Why it works.
Everyone's memory is fallible, and we know it, which is why gaslighting works.
Memories are rebuilt each time we recall them and can be nudged by other people's accounts.
So when someone we trust confidently insists we're wrong, again and again, it's natural to doubt ourselves.
It is most powerful where power is unequal or dependence is deep: partners, parents, bosses.
A parent may tell a child their feelings are wrong.
A manager may deny giving instructions, then blame an employee for following them.
The more isolated someone is, the fewer people they have to check reality with.
Some writers also use the term for institutions that deny documented problems, though that use is more debated.
What it isn't.
The word is now used loosely.
Remembering an argument differently, being corrected when you really erred, or someone lying once to get out of trouble isn't gaslighting.
It is a pattern of deliberately or habitually undermining someone's grip on reality so the other person gains control.
A useful question is whether disagreements consistently leave one person more confused, dependent and less confident.
Over time, people who are gaslit often describe constant self-doubt, excessive apologising, confusion, trouble making small decisions and withdrawing from friends.
Gaslighting is a common feature of coercive control, a pattern of domestic abuse.
Using the term too casually makes it harder to take seriously when it really happens.
Supporting someone else.
If you think a friend or relative is being gaslit, the most useful thing is often simply to stay in their life.
Listen without judging, and tell them what you notice, calmly and specifically: 'I was there, and I remember it the way you do.'
That outside reality check is exactly what gaslighting tries to remove.
Avoid ultimatums or attacking their partner, which can push them to defend the relationship.
Let them make their own decisions, and make sure they know where help is.
Services like 1800RESPECT also advise friends and family, not only the person directly affected.
Keeping your footing.
If you suspect gaslighting, write things down with dates soon after they happen, or keep messages and emails, so you have a record to trust.
Store them somewhere safe that the other person can't access.
Talk to people outside the relationship who can offer a reality check.
Notice patterns, such as always ending up apologising.
You don't need to win every argument about what happened; you can simply say 'I remember it differently' and leave it.
Counsellors can help you rebuild confidence, and 1800RESPECT, 1800 737 732, offers free, confidential support in Australia.
In an emergency, call 000.
The key idea: Gaslighting is a pattern of manipulation that makes someone doubt their own memory and judgement, named after a 1938 play.
Part three. The dark triad.
Narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy: the three 'dark' personality traits psychologists study, and why they're more common than you'd think.
Three overlapping traits.
In 2002, psychologists Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams grouped three traits that share a core of callousness and self-interest: narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy.
In this research they are traits everyone has to some degree, not clinical diagnoses.
Most people score low to moderate, and a high score doesn't make someone a criminal or a monster.
People high on all three tend to be charming at first, exploit others when it suits them, and care little about the harm they cause.
The idea caught on fast and has since produced thousands of studies.
Narcissism and Machiavellianism.
Narcissism, named for the Greek youth who fell in love with his reflection, means an inflated self-importance, entitlement and a need for admiration.
High scorers often make great first impressions.
Over time, low empathy and sharp reactions to criticism strain relationships.
Researchers separate bold, attention-seeking grandiose narcissism from anxious, easily wounded vulnerable narcissism.
Narcissistic personality disorder is a separate diagnosis, made only by professionals.
Machiavellianism is named for Niccolò Machiavelli, who argued in The Prince that rulers sometimes must act without mercy or honesty.
High scorers see people as tools, expect the worst of human nature, and flatter or deceive strategically.
It is more calculating and long-term than psychopathy.
The psychopathy trait.
Psychopathy here means a set of traits: shallow emotions, little empathy or guilt, impulsiveness and a hunger for thrills.
Of the three, it is considered the darkest and the most linked to antisocial behaviour.
Clinical psychopathy is assessed by trained professionals, using tools such as Robert Hare's checklist.
It is commonly estimated at around 1% of the general population, and much higher in prisons.
It isn't a formal diagnosis in the main psychiatric manuals.
Many people with some psychopathic traits never commit crimes.
Some research suggests these traits are more common in certain high-pressure leadership roles, though findings vary.
Measured by questionnaire.
Most research relies on questionnaires where people rate statements about themselves, such as the 27-item Short Dark Triad or the 12-item scale nicknamed the Dirty Dozen.
They are quick and cheap, which helped the field grow fast.
They also have limits.
People may not answer honestly, especially about traits linked to deceit.
Very short scales can blur differences between traits.
Critics note that Machiavellianism and psychopathy scores correlate so strongly they may partly measure the same thing.
Read the findings as broad patterns across groups, not as exact portraits of any one person.
The traits seem to come from a mix of genes and environment, and narcissism tends to decline on average from young adulthood to middle age.
They are tendencies on a spectrum, not a fixed type of person.
Success and self-defence.
Confidence and charisma get people noticed, promoted and chosen as leaders, especially at first.
The costs show up later: broken trust, high staff turnover, toxic teams, and ethical or financial scandals.
Some researchers add a fourth trait, everyday sadism, to make a 'dark tetrad'.
To protect yourself, watch how someone treats people who can't help them, like waiters, cleaners or junior staff.
Be wary of fast flattery, stories where they're always the victim or hero, rules that apply to everyone but them, and no genuine apology.
Avoid armchair diagnoses; only a qualified professional can assess a personality disorder.
Focus on behaviour, keep your boundaries clear, and give trust gradually as it's earned.
The key idea: The dark triad is narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy, measured as traits everyone has to some degree.
Part four. How cults recruit.
Nobody joins a cult.
People join a friendly group with answers, and the rest happens slowly.
Not who you'd expect.
It's tempting to think only foolish or broken people join cults.
Research and survivor accounts suggest otherwise.
Many members are educated, curious and idealistic, often recruited at transitional moments: starting university, moving cities, a breakup, a job loss or grief.
At those times, people look for connection and direction.
Cults don't advertise themselves as cults.
They offer friendship, meaning, purpose and certainty, things everyone wants.
Researchers often prefer the term 'high-control group', because the same dynamics can appear in religious, political, wellness, business and online communities.
The pull is human, not stupid.
Small steps, bigger asks.
Recruitment starts with something harmless: a free course, a meditation class, a Bible study or a friendly dinner.
Newcomers get intense attention and affection, sometimes called love bombing.
Requests start small, like attending another session, then grow into more time, money and loyalty.
Each step feels like a minor extension of the last.
Psychologists call this the foot-in-the-door technique.
In a classic 1966 study, people who first agreed to a small request were much more likely to agree to a big one later.
The full beliefs are often revealed only once people are deeply involved.
Control and the leader.
Robert Lifton, who studied 'thought reform' in the 1950s, and later Steven Hassan, described patterns of control.
Schedules fill with group activity, leaving little energy to reflect.
Outside information is portrayed as dangerous.
Special jargon makes it harder to think in outside terms.
Contact with doubting family and friends is discouraged, and doubts are framed as personal failings.
Most such groups revolve around a leader claiming unique insight.
Questioning is treated as betrayal, and rules may not apply to the leader.
History offers tragic examples: more than 900 followers of Jim Jones died at Jonestown in 1978.
Australia's own, The Family, led by Anne Hamilton-Byrne, raised children in isolation near Melbourne.
Why it works, why stay.
None of this needs hypnosis.
We like to act consistently with past choices.
We look to others to judge what's normal.
And we hate holding beliefs that clash with our actions, which Leon Festinger called cognitive dissonance.
In When Prophecy Fails, 1956, he described a group whose predicted end of the world didn't come.
Some became more committed, not less, because admitting error meant their sacrifices were wasted.
The same forces keep people in.
Leaving can mean losing your whole social world, your purpose and years of investment.
Members may be told terrible things happen to those who leave.
Some have given away savings or worked unpaid for years.
The more someone has sacrificed, the stronger the need to believe it was worth it.
Warning signs and help.

Warning signs include pressure to commit quickly, a leader beyond criticism, us-versus-them thinking, secret teachings revealed in stages, large demands for money or unpaid labour, discouraged outside contact, and punished doubt.
No single sign proves harm, but several together are a real concern.
Healthy groups let you ask hard questions, keep outside friends, see where money goes, and leave without being shunned or threatened.
If someone you love is involved, staying warmly connected gives them a door back.
Direct attacks usually backfire.
Ask genuine questions, share memories, and avoid ultimatums.
Former members may need time and support, and a counsellor or GP is a good start.
For coercive control or abuse, call 1800RESPECT, 1800 737 732; in danger, call 000.
The key idea: People who join cults are often intelligent, educated and idealistic, recruited at vulnerable moments of change.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is a useful test for manipulation?
Answer. Whether it works even when fully understood.
Question two. Which of these is a common gaslighting tactic?
Answer. Flatly denying things that happened.
Question three. In dark triad research, how are the three traits usually treated?
Answer. As traits everyone has to some degree.
Question four. When are people often recruited into cults?
Answer. During life changes such as grief or moving.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
